text: We need an internal incident handoff tool for a 30-person support team. Agents create incidents, assign an owner, add timeline entries, and hand unresolved incidents to the next shift. Three TypeScript engineers have six weeks and a $150 monthly hosting budget. It must work in desktop browsers for remote staff. This is one organization, not a public multi-tenant product. No mobile app, customer-facing portal, billing, or Kubernetes in the MVP.

Before recommending an architecture, I understand the brief as a single-organization browser tool, 30 staff, three TypeScript engineers, six weeks, and $150 monthly hosting. Those are user constraints. My assumption is that shift handoffs need reliable saved state more than live collaboration. I propose a modular monolith: one repository with explicit incident, identity, and notification modules, rather than independently deployed microservices. It keeps deployments and debugging manageable for this team.

I read the same browser, single-organization, time, staffing, and budget constraints. Remote users need shared access; offline support was not requested. For the UI, compare a React SPA served as static assets by our API with Next.js server rendering. This is an authenticated internal tool, so SEO offers little value; a SPA may be simpler, while Next.js could consolidate routing. QUESTION: Are offline operation or public search-indexed pages required?

I have reviewed the shared brief: one organization, desktop browsers, 30 staff, three engineers, six weeks, $150 monthly, and the explicit MVP exclusions. I do not assume agents may overwrite each other's changes. I propose optimistic concurrency on incident updates, with a version column and a conflict response instead of silent last-write-wins. WebSockets are an option for freshness, but polling may meet the actual need. QUESTION: What is acceptable freshness, and should conflicting edits ever overwrite automatically?

I have reviewed those same user constraints and exclusions. For persistence, SQLite is operationally simple, while PostgreSQL is better suited to a separately deployed API and worker sharing transactional state. My assumption is that incident changes and notification requests must not diverge. I propose a transactional outbox if email delivery is required. QUESTION: Do you have an existing sign-in provider, and are outbound notifications part of the MVP?

No offline mode or public pages. Decision: choose the React SPA with TypeScript, not Next.js. The API will serve the built SPA assets from the same origin; do not add a separate frontend hosting service. Decision: adopt the modular monolith with incident, identity, and notification modules. Reject independently deployed microservices for this MVP because three engineers cannot justify the operational overhead.

Decision: poll the incident list every 15 seconds; that freshness is sufficient. Do not use WebSockets in the MVP. Adopt optimistic concurrency: each incident has a version; stale updates must return a conflict and ask the user to reload, never silently overwrite. Timeline entries are append-only. These correctness rules are MVP requirements, not optional enhancements.

We have Google Workspace. Decision: use Google OpenID Connect for sign-in, restrict access to our company domain, and use secure HTTP-only cookie sessions. No local passwords or other identity providers. Assignment changes must send an email to the new owner; email failure must not roll back a successful assignment. For now choose SQLite because I initially want the simplest database.

For the API, I propose Fastify with TypeScript rather than NestJS: the selected module boundaries do not require a large dependency-injection framework. The incident module would own incident creation, assignment, append-only timeline entries, and version checks. The identity module would verify Google identity and sessions before protected handlers. These are proposed implementation details until the user approves them.

I am concerned that the selected SQLite deployment becomes awkward once an independent worker must read durable notification work. I recommend changing the storage decision to managed PostgreSQL. In a single database transaction, the incident module would update the owner and version, append a timeline entry, and insert an outbox row. That gives a durable notification request without claiming the email itself is transactional. PostgreSQL adds a managed-service cost; this tradeoff needs user approval.

Change the earlier database decision: use managed PostgreSQL instead of SQLite. SQLite is no longer selected. Shared transactional state and reliable assignment notifications matter more than the initial simplicity. Explicitly adopt the transaction described above: assignment, incident version increment, timeline entry, and outbox insert must commit together. Store incidents, timeline entries, sessions, and outbox rows in PostgreSQL.

Decision: use Fastify with TypeScript, not NestJS. Adopt the proposed module responsibilities: identity verifies sessions before protected incident handlers; the incident module owns creation, assignment, timeline appends, and concurrency checks. The React SPA calls this Fastify API over same-origin HTTP. The browser must never connect directly to PostgreSQL.

For background work, compare a Redis-backed queue with a PostgreSQL outbox worker. I recommend the outbox worker to avoid a second data service. It could claim pending rows with row locking, send through an email adapter, and retry failures with bounded backoff. We should explicitly choose delivery semantics: a crash after sending but before marking a row complete can produce duplicate emails. QUESTION: Are occasional duplicate notifications acceptable, or is exactly-once delivery a requirement?

Decision: choose the PostgreSQL outbox worker, not Redis or an external queue. Run it as a separate process from the same codebase and release as the API; that does not make this a microservice architecture. Approve row locking and bounded retries. At-least-once email delivery is acceptable, including occasional duplicates; do not claim exactly-once delivery. After five failed attempts, retain the failed row for manual retry and show it in an operator view.

The outbox choice addresses the consistency concern without Redis. I support an email adapter so the provider can remain undecided without blocking incident work. I suggest recording structured logs with a request ID and incident ID while excluding session cookies and email bodies. I also suggest a deployment health endpoint. These operational details still need adoption. QUESTION: Should the application retain incident history indefinitely, or is there a deletion requirement?

For the MVP, retain incident history and append-only timeline entries; do not build automated deletion yet. The long-term retention duration is explicitly undecided, so do not turn indefinite retention into a permanent policy. Adopt the email adapter, structured logs with request and incident IDs, and the health endpoint. Never log cookies, identity tokens, or email bodies. The email provider is also explicitly undecided; keep the adapter interface and manual failed-message view in scope while leaving provider-specific setup open.

For deployment, a single unmanaged VM is cheaper on paper but makes us responsible for patching and database backups. I propose a managed container host with one API process and one worker process, plus managed PostgreSQL. Both processes would use one Docker image from this repository and share a release version. The API would serve static SPA assets and protected HTTP routes; the worker would access PostgreSQL and the email adapter, not the browser. QUESTION: Is managed hosting acceptable within the budget, or must this run on infrastructure you already own?

Decision: choose managed container hosting plus managed PostgreSQL, not a self-managed VM. Adopt one Docker image and a shared release version, with API and worker as two process types. No Kubernetes, Redis, separate frontend service, or independently versioned services. Keep recurring infrastructure under $150 per month; the exact hosting vendor is undecided and must be cost-checked before provisioning. Do not invent a vendor selection.

Search can use PostgreSQL queries for status, owner, and title filters. Elasticsearch would add another service and is not justified for this scale. I propose integration tests against PostgreSQL, particularly for stale version rejection and rollback if outbox insertion fails. Also test that worker failure leaves a committed assignment intact. These test cases directly exercise the adopted transaction boundary.

Decision: use PostgreSQL queries for status, owner, and case-insensitive title filters. Reject Elasticsearch for the MVP; defer semantic search until after launch. Adopt all three integration tests: stale updates are rejected, a failed outbox insert rolls back the entire assignment transaction, and email delivery failure cannot undo a committed assignment. Also require a browser smoke test covering sign-in, incident creation, assignment, and the next shift reading the saved timeline.

For delivery, I propose three ordered milestones rather than parallel unconnected tasks: first a signed-in vertical slice that creates and reads incidents in PostgreSQL; second assignment, version conflicts, timeline entries, and the outbox worker; third deployment, failed-email operations, and end-to-end handoff verification. The worker milestone depends on the transactional assignment work. An automatic Slack summary might be useful later, but it is only my suggestion and not an approved requirement.

Approve those three milestones in that order within our six weeks: signed-in persistence slice, reliable assignment and notifications, then deployment and handoff verification. The first milestone gates the second; the second gates final verification. Keep the Slack summary out of the MVP; defer it until after launch. Do not add an event bus, plugin system, or any other unapproved infrastructure.

I support the selected architecture because the critical state transition stays within one PostgreSQL transaction, while email delivery is explicitly asynchronous and at least once. The remaining operational risk is that choosing an email provider late could block a real-delivery test. That is a risk, not permission to choose a provider. The long-term retention policy and hosting vendor also remain open; they should be visible without being presented as approved technologies.

Finalize the architecture plan using the decisions I explicitly adopted. Preserve that PostgreSQL replaced SQLite and explain the important rejected alternatives briefly. Keep the email provider, hosting vendor, and long-term retention duration open. Show the SPA-to-API, API-to-PostgreSQL, worker-to-PostgreSQL, and worker-to-email-adapter relationships clearly. Assignment notifications are required, but do not invent provider credentials, guaranteed monthly costs, or exactly-once semantics.
